items.title: Elizabeth I's wardrobe was a political instrument
items.claim: How extensive was Elizabeth I's wardrobe at her death?

options.text: A modest collection of state robes

Inventories at her death (1603) recorded around 2,000 gowns, gifts and ceremonial robes; she owned around 80 wigs after smallpox scarring in 1562 and used ceruse make-up to maintain the 'Mask of Youth' image

items.reveal:
Elizabeth survived smallpox in October 1562 with scarring on her face and neck. Ceruse (white lead and vinegar) gave the white complexion seen in portraits — slowly toxic with long-term use.

Nicholas Hilliard's 'Treatise Concerning the Arte of Limning' (1598-1602) reports that painters were instructed not to show shadow on the queen's face after about 1590 — the 'Mask of Youth' image preserved her as eternally young.

The wardrobe was renewed by gifts from courtiers, who chose colours, materials and embroidered devices loaded with political meaning. Roy Strong's 'Gloriana' (1987) catalogued the visual programme.
items.why: Elizabethan court politics was conducted partly through clothes. The 'Virgin Queen' image was constructed by carefully managed wardrobe, portraiture and pageant — a sustained branding exercise of the monarchy.

items.title: Tutankhamun was minor — fame comes from an intact tomb
items.claim: Why is Tutankhamun (r. c. 1332-1323 BCE) so famous?

options.text: He was the greatest of all New Kingdom pharaohs
He was a young, minor pharaoh whose tomb (KV62) was found nearly intact by Howard Carter on 4 November 1922 — almost the only royal tomb to escape ancient looting
He led the Egyptians to defeat the Hittites
He was the first pharaoh to build a pyramid

items.reveal:
Tutankhamun died around age 19 after a reign of about 9 years. He partially reversed his father Akhenaten's religious reforms but his reign was historically minor.

Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, found a single step on 4 November 1922 after years of fruitless digging. On 26 November he made a small hole, held up a candle, and when asked if he could see anything famously replied 'Yes, wonderful things'. The tomb contained over 5,000 artefacts. Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite in April 1923, fuelling 'curse' stories.
items.why: Fame is not the same as historical importance. Tutankhamun's celebrity is an artefact of preservation and 20th-century media, not of what he actually did.

items.title: The Hundred Years War lasted 116 years
items.claim: When did the Hundred Years War begin and end?

options.text: 1337 (Edward III claims the French throne) to 1453 (Battle of Castillon) — 116 years, with long truces in between

items.reveal_title: A name invented in the 19th century
items.reveal:
The phrase 'Hundred Years War' was coined by French historians in the 1860s. Contemporaries did not see it as a single conflict but as a series of campaigns separated by long peaces (e.g. the Treaty of Brétigny, 1360).

Major English victories: Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356), Agincourt (1415). Major French recoveries: Du Guesclin's reconquests under Charles V, and Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans (1429). It ended with the French victory at Castillon in 1453 — three months before Constantinople fell.
items.why: Periodisation is a historical choice, not a fact. A '100 years' war that was actually 116, mostly truce, and named four centuries later is a useful reminder.
